![Image from [The New Yorker](https://www.newyorker.com/culture/annals-of-inquiry/its-possible-to-learn-in-our-sleep-should-we).](cover.jpg){fig-align="center"}

[Shayla Love](https://www.newyorker.com/contributors/shayla-love)'s [New Yorker piece](https://www.newyorker.com/culture/annals-of-inquiry/its-possible-to-learn-in-our-sleep-should-we) [[1]](#ref-1) revisits sleep learning, a field that a mid-1950s paper by Charles W. Simon and William H. Emmons [[2]](#ref-2) effectively condemned as quackery by showing that the subjects in most earlier studies had simply been awake. Decades of neglect later, modern electroencephalography (EEG) has let researchers run the experiments properly. The article reports findings from [Ken Paller](https://faculty.wcas.northwestern.edu/paller/)'s lab at Northwestern, [Karen Konkoly](https://www.psychol.cam.ac.uk/staff/dr-karen-konkoly) (now at Cambridge), [Anat Arzi](https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=z7i2LKcAAAAJ) at the Weizmann Institute, [Emma Peters](https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=eyXo3hUAAAAJ) at Bern, [Martin Dresler](https://dreslerlab.org/) at the Donders Institute, and [Thomas Andrillon](https://thomas-andrillon.wixsite.com/research) at the Paris Brain Institute.

What the article reports:

- Konkoly's 2026 study in *Neuroscience of Consciousness* [[3]](#ref-3) gave spatial puzzles to twenty lucid dreamers, paired each puzzle with a specific sound cue, and tracked which ones surfaced in dreams. Participants solved 42% of puzzles that appeared in dreams and 17% of ones that did not, with the highest solve rates coming from ordinary rather than lucid dreams.
- Independent labs in the US, France, Germany, and the Netherlands [[4]](#ref-4) have established two-way communication with sleeping lucid dreamers, delivering yes/no questions and arithmetic and receiving eye-movement responses, all while EEG confirmed the participants were not awake.
- Anat Arzi's 2014 Weizmann study [[5]](#ref-5) found that smokers exposed to a cigarette-plus-rotting-fish scent pairing overnight reduced cigarette consumption by more than 30%, more than a matched awake group.
- Emma Peters's work with lucid dreamers [[6]](#ref-6) shows that practicing physical tasks (finger tapping, coin tossing, dart throwing with the non-dominant hand) inside a dream improves next-day performance versus controls, with the important caveat that dreams are not a controlled practice environment.
- Paller and Andrillon both caution against the obvious commercial reading. A recent paper from Paller's group [[7]](#ref-7) shows that targeted memory reactivation depends on ample, undisturbed slow-wave sleep, and when the cueing itself fragments sleep it undermines the consolidation it was meant to help. Andrillon: dreams "follow their own rules and presumably serve their own inexplicable aims." Konkoly has started describing the push to instrument sleep as trying to "colonize" it with "wake-centric values."

## My Notes

- The puzzle finding is worth taking seriously because of the within-subject design. Each participant served as their own control on whether a puzzle surfaced in a dream, which rules out individual ability and motivation. The scent-pairing and motor-practice results rest on between-group comparisons that don't. External validity is still the usual lucid-dreamer caveat: the participant pool doesn't generalize to the population.
- Puzzles were solved at a higher rate when they appeared in ordinary rather than lucid dreams. If that holds up, it undercuts the intuitive assumption that the useful state for cognitive work is the one closest to wakefulness. The looser, non-self-aware mode may be doing something the metacognitively-aware mode interferes with. That's the opposite of how consumer products for sleep optimization are usually pitched.
- Andrillon's warning about "colonizing" sleep with "wake-centric values" lines up with [Vivienne Ming's WSJ piece on AI cannibalizing human intelligence](/posts/20260426-ai-cannibalizing-human-intelligence/). Both describe a failure mode where a restorative or generative process gets taken over by productivity goals and quietly degrades. Sleep sits in the same place as unaided cognition in Ming's argument: a working system whose value is hard to see from outside, which is why the colonization pitch is so easy to make.
- Every study here acts on material the subject already touched awake. Sleep reworked that material; it didn't acquire it from scratch. The old Psycho-phone pitch was the "from scratch" version, and none of the current work supports it.
